questions.label: Exercise 1
questions.text:
Exercise 1
A class in advanced physics is composed of 10 juniors, 30 seniors, and 10 graduate students. The final
grades show that 3 of the juniors, 10 of the seniors, and 5 of the graduate students received an A for the
course. If a student is chosen at random from this class and is found to have earned an A, what is the
probability that he or she is a senior?
questions.modelAnswer:
Let $A$ : student earned an A; $B$ : student is senior. Then we want $P(B|A)$. So:

$$P(B|A)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(A)}=\frac{\frac{10}{50}}{\frac{18}{50}}=\frac{10}{18}$$

questions.label: Exercise 4(a)
questions.sharedContext:
Exercise 4
 In the senior year of a high school graduating class of 100 students, 42 studied mathematics, 68 studied
psychology, 54 studied history, 22 studied both mathematics and history, 25 studied both mathematics
and psychology, 7 studied history but neither mathematics nor psychology, 10 studied all three subjects,
and 8 did not take any of the three. Randomly select a student from the class and find the probability
of the following events.
questions.text: a) A person enrolled in psychology takes all three subjects
questions.modelAnswer:
Let $H$, $M$ and $P$ denote a person taking history, mathematics, and psychology, respectively.

$$P(M\cap P\cap H)=\frac{10}{68}=\frac{5}{34}$$

questions.label: Exercise 4(b)
questions.sharedContext:
Exercise 4
 In the senior year of a high school graduating class of 100 students, 42 studied mathematics, 68 studied
psychology, 54 studied history, 22 studied both mathematics and history, 25 studied both mathematics
and psychology, 7 studied history but neither mathematics nor psychology, 10 studied all three subjects,
and 8 did not take any of the three. Randomly select a student from the class and find the probability
of the following events.
questions.text: b) A person not taking psychology is taking both history and mathematics
questions.modelAnswer:
Let $H$, $M$ and $P$ denote a person taking history, mathematics, and psychology, respectively.

$$P(M\cap H\mid P')=\frac{P(M\cap H\cap P')}{P(P')}=\frac{22-10}{100-68}=\frac{12}{32}=\frac{3}{8}$$

questions.label: Exercise 6(a)
questions.sharedContext:
Exercise 6
 The probability that a married man watches a certain television show is 0.45, and the probability
that a married woman watches the show is 0.5. The probability that a man watches the show, given
that his wife does, is 0.8. Find the probability that
questions.text: a) a married couple watches the show;
questions.modelAnswer:
Consider the events: $H$ husband watches a certain show, and $W$ denotes that the wife watches the
same show.

$$P(W\cap H)=P(W)\cdot P(H\mid W)=0.5\cdot 0.8=0.4$$

$$P(W\cup H)=P(W)+P(H)-P(W\cap H)=0.5+0.45-0.4=0.55$$

questions.label: Exercise 8
questions.text:
Exercise 8
 A paint-store chain produces and sells latex and semigloss paint. Based on long-range sales, the
probability that a customer will purchase latex paint is 0.75. Of those that purchase latex paint, 60%
also purchase rollers. But only 30% of semigloss paint buyers purchase rollers. A randomly selected
buyer purchases a roller and a can of paint. What is the probability that the paint is latex?
questions.modelAnswer:
Consider the events: $A$ denotes a customer purchasing latex paint, $A'$ denotes a customer purchasing
semigloss paint, and $B$ denotes a customer purchasing rollers.

$$P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(B\mid A)\cdot P(A)}{P(B\mid A)\cdot P(A)+P(B\mid A')\cdot P(A')}=\frac{0.60\cdot 0.75}{0.60\cdot 0.75+0.25\cdot 0.30}=0.857$$

questions.label: Exercise 9
questions.text:
Exercise 9
 Denote by A, B, and C the events that a grand prize is behind doors A, B, and C, respectively.
Suppose you randomly picked a door, say A. The game host opened a door, say B, and showed there
was no prize behind it. Now the host offers you the option of either staying at the door that you picked
(A) or switching to the remaining unopened door (C). Use probability to explain whether you should
switch or not.
questions.modelAnswer:
If we use the assumptions that the host would not open the door you picked nor the door with the prize
behind it, we can use Bayes rule to solve the problem. First, observe that $P(A)=P(B)=P(C)=\frac{1}{3}$.
Denote by $H$ the event that you picked door $A$ and the host opened door $B$, while there is no prize
behind the door $B$. Then

$$P(A\mid H)=\frac{P(H\mid A)\cdot P(A)}{P(H\mid A)\cdot P(A)+P(H\mid B)\cdot P(B)+P(H\mid C)\cdot P(C)}$$

$$=\frac{P(H\mid A)}{P(H\mid A)+P(H\mid B)+P(H\mid C)}=\frac{\frac{1}{2}}{\frac{1}{2}+0+1}=\frac{1}{3}.$$

The intuition is as follows: since the player initially chose door A, the chance that the host opens door
B is 1/2 if the prize is behind door A, 0 if the prize is behind door B, and 1 if the prize is behind door
C. Given the outcome, you should switch doors.

questions.label: Exercise 10
questions.text:
Exercise 10
 Every morning during college weeks, a period of 6 weeks, a student rolls a die. If the outcome is a
six, then he will study; otherwise he goes back to sleep. During examination week, rather than rolling a
die, our student flips a coin and he will study if he flips heads. If our student is studying one morning,
what is the probability that it is examination week?
questions.modelAnswer:
$E$ : Exam week $S$ : Studying. We have $P(E)=\frac{1}{7}$, $P(S|E)=\frac{1}{2}$ and $P(S|E')=\frac{1}{6}$. So $P(E\cap S)=P(E)\cdot P(S|E)=\frac{1}{14}$ and $P(E'\cap S)=P(E')\cdot P(S|E')=\frac{6}{7}\cdot \frac{1}{6}=\frac{1}{7}$. Hence

$$P(E|S)=\frac{P(E\cap S)}{P(S)}=\frac{\frac{1}{14}}{\frac{1}{14}+\frac{1}{7}}=\frac{1}{3}$$

questions.label: Exercise 11
questions.text:
Exercise 11
 A truth serum has the property that 90 % of the guilty suspects are properly judged while, of course,
10 % of the guilty suspects are improperly found innocent. On the other hand, innocent suspects are
misjudged 1 % of the time. If the suspect was selected from a group of suspects of which only 5 % have
ever committed a crime, and the serum indicates that he is guilty, what is the probability that he is
innocent?
questions.modelAnswer:
$G$ : Guilty $F$ : Found guilty. We are interested in $P(G' |F)$.
We have $P(G)=0.05$, $P(F |G)=0.90$ and $P(F |G')=0.01$. So $P(F\cap G)=P(G)\cdot P(F |G)=0.05\cdot 0.90=0.045$ and $P(F\cap G')=P(G')\cdot P(F |G')=0.95\cdot 0.01=0.0095$. So $P(F)=P(F\cap G)+P(F\cap G')=0.045+0.0095=0.0545$. Hence

$$P(G' |F)=\frac{P(F\cap G')}{P(F)}=\frac{0.0095}{0.0545}=0.174$$

questions.label: Exercise 12(a)
questions.sharedContext:
Exercise 12
 A large industrial firm uses three local motels to provide overnight accomodations for its clients.
From past experience it is know that 20% of the clients are assigned rooms at the Ramada Inn, 50% at
the Sheraton, and 30% at the Lakeview Motor Lodge. If the plumbing is faulty in 5% of the rooms at
the Ramadan Inn, in 4% of the rooms at the Sheraton, and in 8% of the rooms in the Lakeview Motor
Lodge, what is the probability that
questions.text: a) a client will be assigned a room with faulty plumbing?
questions.modelAnswer:
Let $R$, $S$, and $L$ resperesnt the events that a client is assigned a room at the Ramada Inn, Sheraton,
and Lakeview Motor Lodge, respectively, and let $F$ represent the event that the plumbing is faulty.

$$P(F)=P(F\mid R)P(R)+P(F\mid S)P(S)+P(F\mid L)P(L)=0.05\cdot 0.2+0.04\cdot 0.4+0.08\cdot 0.3=0.054.$$

questions.label: Exercise 13
questions.text:
Exercise 13
 A certain form of cancer is known to be found in women over 60 with probability 0.06, A blood test
exists for the detection of the disease, but the test is not infallible. In fact, it is known that 10% of the
time, the test gives a false negative and 5% of the time the test gives a false positive. If a woman over
60 is known to have taken the test and received a favorable (i.e., negative) result, what is the probability
that she has the disease?
questions.modelAnswer:
Consider the events: $C$ denotes that a woman over 60 has cancer and $P$ denotes that the test gives
a positive result. So $P(C)=0.06$, $P(P' | C)=0.1$ and $P(P | C')=0.05$.

$$P(C\mid P')=\frac{P(P'\mid C)P(C)}{P(P'\mid C)P(C)+P(P'\mid C')P(C')}=\frac{0.1\cdot 0.06}{0.1\cdot 0.06+(1-0.05)(1-0.06)}=0.0067$$

questions.label: Exercise 14
questions.text:
Exercise 14
 A firm is accustomed to training operators who do certain tasks on a production line. Those operators
who attend the training course are known to be able to meet their production quotas 90% of the time.
New operators who do not take the training course only meet their quotas 65% of the time. Forty percent
of new operators attend the course. Given that a new operator meets her production quota, what is the
probability that she attended the program?
questions.modelAnswer:
Consider the events: $T$ denotes that an operator is trained, so $P(T)=0.4$, and $M$ denotes an operator
meets quota, $P(M | T)=0.9$ and $P(M | T')=0.65$.

$$P(T\mid M)=\frac{P(M\mid T)P(T)}{P(M\mid T)P(T)+P(M\mid T')P(T')}=\frac{0.9\cdot 0.4}{0.9\cdot 0.4+0.65\cdot 0.6}=0.48$$
